title: How do you ensure a Terraform change does NOT unexpectedly recreate resources — read the plan for create/update/destroy/replace, know which attributes are immutable (force replacement) vs updatable in place, pin provider and module versions, review plans in PRs, use `lifecycle` rules (e.g. `prevent_destroy`/`ignore_changes`) carefully, and treat IaC as a controlled change process rather than "plan and apply"?
shortTitle: Ensuring a Terraform change does NOT unexpectedly recreate resources

s1_definition.profdef: Preventing unexpected recreation means combining several disciplines: reading the plan to distinguish create, update-in-place, destroy, and replace actions; knowing which resource attributes are immutable and therefore force replacement when changed; pinning provider and module versions so defaults do not shift under you; reviewing every plan in a pull request; and applying `lifecycle` blocks such as `prevent_destroy` and `ignore_changes` deliberately. Together these turn "plan and apply" into a controlled change process with explicit guardrails.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India treats changing live infrastructure like moving money between Rajesh's and Priya's accounts — every step is checked, logged, and approved, never done casually. Before any change touches the vault, a second officer reads the instruction slip (the plan) and asks "does this just update a record, or does it empty and recreate the account?" If it would recreate the account, they put a hard lock on it (prevent_destroy) so the system physically refuses. Some fields on the account change outside the bank's control, like an auto-updated timestamp, and the bank tells the system to ignore those so they do not trigger a pointless rewrite (ignore_changes).
s1_definition.oneliner: Read the plan, know which attributes are immutable, pin versions, review in PRs, and guard stateful resources with prevent_destroy — IaC is a controlled change process, not "plan and apply."
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Preventing unexpected recreation means combining several disciplines: reading the plan to distinguish create, update-in-place, destroy, and replace actions; knowing which resource attributes are immutable and therefore force replacement when changed; pinning provider and module versions so defaults do not shift under you; reviewing every plan in a pull request; and applying `lifecycle` blocks such as `prevent_destroy` and `ignore_changes` deliberately. Together these turn "plan and apply" into a controlled change process with explicit guardrails.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India treats changing live infrastructure like moving money between Rajesh's and Priya's accounts — every step is checked, logged, and approved, never done casually. Before any change touches the vault, a second officer reads the instruction slip (the plan) and asks "does this just update a record, or does it empty and recreate the account?" If it would recreate the account, they put a hard lock on it (prevent_destroy) so the system physically refuses. Some fields on the account change outside the bank's control, like an auto-updated timestamp, and the bank tells the system to ignore those so they do not trigger a pointless rewrite (ignore_changes).

**One line to remember:** Read the plan, know which attributes are immutable, pin versions, review in PRs, and guard stateful resources with prevent_destroy — IaC is a controlled change process, not "plan and apply."

sections.s2_technical:
The first line of defence is simply reading the plan carefully. Terraform prints `+` for create, `~` for update in place, `-` for destroy, and `-/+` for replace. Next to a replacement it annotates the exact attribute with `# forces replacement`. If you only glance at "Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change" you can miss that the one change is actually a destroy-and-recreate of something critical.

The second defence is knowing which attributes are immutable. Immutable attributes are ones the cloud API cannot change on an existing object, so Terraform must replace the whole resource. Common examples are an EC2 instance's `availability_zone`, an RDS instance's `engine`, a subnet's `cidr_block`, an S3 bucket's `bucket` name, and many `name` fields. Mutable attributes like `tags`, `instance_class` on some resources, or security-group `description` can usually be updated in place. Reading the provider documentation tells you which is which, and the plan confirms it.

The third defence is pinning versions. A provider upgrade can change a default or recompute an attribute, which silently turns a no-op into a replacement. By pinning `required_providers` and the module `version`, and by only upgrading deliberately, you remove this whole class of surprise. The fourth defence is process: every change goes through a pull request where a `terraform plan` is attached, a second engineer reads it, and a policy tool such as OPA or Sentinel can automatically fail the pipeline if it sees a destroy of a tagged-critical resource.

The fifth defence is the `lifecycle` block, used carefully. `prevent_destroy = true` makes Terraform error out rather than destroy that resource, which is perfect for production databases — but it also blocks legitimate destroys, so you remove it consciously when you really mean to delete. `ignore_changes = [tags["LastModified"]]` tells Terraform to stop fighting over attributes that something outside Terraform mutates, which prevents endless spurious diffs. `create_before_destroy = true` flips the order of a replacement so the new resource is built before the old one is removed, eliminating downtime when replacement is unavoidable. The danger is overusing `ignore_changes` — if you ignore too much, real drift goes unnoticed.

A senior nuance: when a replacement is being forced only because of a cosmetic rename or a provider recompute, you often do not want to replace at all. `terraform state mv` renames a resource in state without recreating it, and `terraform plan -refresh-only` lets you reconcile state with reality without proposing changes. Treating these as everyday tools is what separates "plan and apply" from a real change process.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India stores customer statements in an S3 bucket and runs the payments service on an EC2 instance, both managed by Terraform. An engineer wants to move the payments EC2 instance to a different availability zone for better latency, and separately wants to rename the statements bucket resource in code for clarity.

Problem 1 — Changing the EC2 `availability_zone` is immutable, so the plan shows `-/+`. If the engineer does not notice, the running payments instance that processes transfers from Rajesh SAV2001 to Priya CUR3001 would be destroyed and recreated, dropping in-flight requests. The guard here is reading the plan and using `create_before_destroy` so a new instance is up before the old one dies.

Problem 2 — Renaming the bucket resource block in HCL makes Terraform think the old resource is gone and a new one should be created, proposing to destroy the statements bucket (data loss). The guard is `prevent_destroy = true`, which makes Terraform refuse, plus using `terraform state mv` to rename without recreating.

Problem 3 — An external backup job keeps adding a `LastBackup` tag to the bucket, so every plan shows a spurious tag change. The guard is `ignore_changes = [tags["LastBackup"]]`.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `ChangeGuard` that, given a `PlannedResource` describing the action, whether the resource is protected, whether create-before-destroy is set, and which tags are ignored, decides whether to allow, block, or safely sequence the change. Classes: `PlannedResource`, `LifecyclePolicy`, `ChangeGuard` with `evaluate()`, and a `RecreationGuardDemo` main.

##### 4c. Configuration File — the real Terraform lifecycle guards

```hcl
# terraform/payments.tf

resource "aws_instance" "payments" {
  ami               = var.ami_id
  instance_type     = "c6i.xlarge"
  availability_zone = var.az            # immutable: changing this forces -/+

  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true        # build new instance BEFORE killing old one
  }
  tags = { service = "payments" }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "statements" {
  bucket = "nbi-customer-statements-prod"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true              # Terraform ERRORS rather than destroy this
    ignore_changes  = [tags["LastBackup"]]  # stop fighting the external backup job
  }
}
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.iac.RecreationGuardDemo

# Real-world techniques this demonstrates:
terraform plan -out=change.plan
terraform show change.plan | grep "forces replacement"   # catch immutable replacements
terraform state mv aws_s3_bucket.old aws_s3_bucket.statements   # rename, NOT recreate
terraform plan -refresh-only                              # reconcile state w/o changes
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a plan with three entries — an EC2 instance being replaced due to an availability-zone change, an S3 bucket being destroyed due to a resource rename, and the same S3 bucket showing a tag diff on the LastBackup tag.

Step 1: The guard evaluates the EC2 instance. The action is REPLACE and the changed attribute is immutable, but the lifecycle policy has create_before_destroy set. The guard returns SEQUENCE, meaning Terraform will build the new payments instance before destroying the old one, so no in-flight transfer between SAV2001 and CUR3001 is dropped.

Step 2: The guard evaluates the S3 destroy. The action is DESTROY and the policy has prevent_destroy set. The guard returns BLOCK and loudly refuses, suggesting terraform state mv to rename the resource in state instead of recreating it, protecting all stored statements.

Step 3: The guard evaluates the S3 tag change. The triggering tag is LastBackup, which the policy ignores. The guard returns SUPPRESS, so the spurious diff from the external backup job never becomes a real change and never produces churn.

Step 4: All three risky changes were intercepted by a different guardrail, so nothing reached production that would have unexpectedly recreated a resource.

```
2026-10-30 01:40:18 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — evaluating plan against recreation guardrails
2026-10-30 01:40:18 [WARNING] SEQUENCE: aws_instance.payments immutable attr forces replace — create_before_destroy builds new BEFORE destroying old (no downtime)
2026-10-30 01:40:18 [SEVERE ] BLOCK: aws_s3_bucket.statements would be DESTROY but prevent_destroy=true — refusing. Use 'terraform state mv' to rename without recreating.
2026-10-30 01:40:18 [INFO   ] SUPPRESS: aws_s3_bucket.statements diff on ignored tag 'LastBackup' — no change proposed
2026-10-30 01:40:18 [INFO   ] Guardrails applied: no unexpected recreation reached production.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Ensuring that a Terraform change does not unexpectedly recreate a resource is about treating infrastructure as a controlled change process rather than a casual plan-and-apply. My first guardrail is reading the plan properly: Terraform prints plus for create, tilde for update in place, minus for destroy, and minus-plus for replace, and it annotates the exact attribute that forces a replacement. I never trust the one-line summary; I read every minus-plus line and ask whether that recreation is acceptable.

My second guardrail is knowing which attributes are immutable. Things like an EC2 instance's availability zone, an RDS engine, a subnet CIDR, or an S3 bucket name cannot be changed in place because the cloud API has no way to mutate them, so Terraform's only option is destroy and recreate. Knowing this lets me anticipate a replacement before I even run the plan. My third guardrail is pinning provider and module versions, because an unpinned provider upgrade can recompute a default and silently turn a no-op into a replacement.

The rest is process and lifecycle rules. Every change goes through a pull request where a plan is attached and a second engineer reviews it, and a policy tool can fail the pipeline automatically if it sees a destroy of a critical resource. I use lifecycle blocks deliberately: prevent_destroy makes Terraform refuse to delete a production resource, create_before_destroy builds a replacement before removing the old one so there is no downtime, and ignore_changes stops Terraform fighting over attributes that something external mutates. In my project at the National Bank of India, moving the payments EC2 instance to a new availability zone forced a replacement, but create_before_destroy meant a new instance was running before the old one died, so no in-flight transfer between Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001 was dropped. Separately, renaming the statements bucket in code would have proposed a destroy, but prevent_destroy refused it and I used terraform state mv to rename in state instead of recreating. And when an external backup job kept adding a LastBackup tag, ignore_changes stopped the endless spurious diffs. The discipline I always state is that read the plan, know your immutable attributes, pin your versions, review in PRs, and guard stateful resources — that combination is what prevents an unexpected recreation.
